Weight
WAYT
n.
Old English wiht, “weight, value.” In Scripture chiefly renders the Hebrew kābōd, “weight, heaviness,” whose substantival use becomes the great word glory—the manifested weight of God; and the Greek baros, “weight, heaviness,” used by Paul in 2 Cor 4:17 of an “eternal weight of glory.”

Biblical Definition

Weight in Scripture is one of the deepest theological metaphors, governing two great clusters of doctrine. First, the glory of God: the Hebrew kābōd literally means “weight, heaviness” before it means “glory.” God’s glory is His manifested weight: the substantial, awe-evoking, ungainsayable substance of who He is, breaking forth in such manifestations as Sinai’s thunder and the cloud filling Solomon’s temple. To glorify God is to give Him weight; to despise Him is to count Him light. The created world is, in Scripture’s view, drained of weight when God is taken out of it: vanity of vanities, all is vanity—the Hebrew hebel, “vapor, breath, lightness,” the opposite of kābōd. To live coram Deo is to live among weighty things; to live as if God were not is to live among vapors. Second, the eschatological weight: Paul in 2 Cor 4:17 sets the present afflictions against a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. The Greek is striking—aionion baros doxes, an eternal heaviness of glory—and the contrast is decisive. The afflictions are light (elaphron, light in weight) and but for a moment; the glory is heavy and forever. The believer’s present troubles, however heavy they feel, are revealed in the eschatological scales as light; the coming glory, however invisible now, is revealed in the same scales as heavy beyond comparison. The weight category therefore organizes much of Christian wisdom. The saint learns to value things by their weight: God Himself heaviest, the soul heavier than the body, eternity heavier than time, the praise of God heavier than the praise of men, the reward of the Father heavier than the rewards of the world, the unseen heavier than the seen. The trained spiritual judgment is, in part, the recovered capacity to feel the true weight of what God has weighted heavily and the true lightness of what He has weighted lightly—and to live accordingly.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WEIGHT as the quantity of a body, ascertained by the balance; heaviness; gravity; that property by which heavy bodies tend toward the center of the earth; figuratively, importance; consequence; moment; pressure.

expand to see more

WEIGHT, n. — 1. The quantity of a body, ascertained by the balance; the quality of being heavy. 2. Heaviness; gravity; that property by which heavy bodies tend toward the center of the earth. 3. Pressure; burden; as the weight of grief. 4. Importance; consequence; moment; impressiveness; power; as, men of weight in society. 5. In scripture, glory; as, an eternal weight of glory (2 Cor 4:17).

WEIGHTY, a. — 1. Having great weight; heavy; ponderous. 2. Important; momentous; as, weighty considerations.

Key Scripture

2 Corinthians 4:17 — "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory."

Exodus 33:18 — "And he said, I beseech thee, shew me thy glory."

Ecclesiastes 1:2 — "Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity."

Hebrews 12:1 — "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us."

Modern Corruption

The biblical category of weight is corrupted by the lightness culture of the digital age, in which the trained capacity to feel what God has weighted heavily (Himself, the soul, eternity) and what He has weighted lightly (this world’s rewards, the praise of men, the moment’s afflictions) has been progressively dulled by a constant stream of trivializing inputs.

expand to see more

The digital age is, in many of its tendencies, the systematic dulling of the soul’s capacity to feel weight. The endless scroll trains the attention to flit from item to item, holding each only briefly, weighting nothing for long; the entertainment register makes the soul accustomed to lightness and uncomfortable with anything heavy; the constant access to trivia drains the spaces in life that previously held weighty considerations (death, eternity, God, the soul) and fills them with the immediate-but-trivial. The believer absorbs the cultural training and brings it to the things God has weighted most heavily, finding himself unable to feel the weight of God Himself, the weight of his own soul, the weight of eternity, the weight of the afflictions of the persecuted, the weight of the souls of the lost. Recover the weight category, and the saint begins to recover the spiritual judgment that lives toward God: God heaviest, the soul heavier than the body, eternity heavier than time, the unseen heavier than the seen.

The discipline of recovery is partly negative and partly positive. Negatively: identify and reduce the lightening inputs—the trivial media, the constant distraction, the perpetual stream of items too small to weight. Positively: deliberately spend time with the heavy things—sustained reading of Scripture, especially the weighty books (Romans, Hebrews, Isaiah, the Psalms); sustained meditation on God’s attributes; sustained reflection on death and eternity; sustained prayer that gives the soul time to feel what it is asking; sustained presence with the dying, the bereaved, the persecuted, whose lives are heavy with realities the comfortable believer has trained himself not to feel. The recovery of weight is the recovery of the capacity Paul exercises in 2 Cor 4:17: to feel that present afflictions, however severe they seem, are light and but for a moment, and that the coming glory, however invisible, is a far more exceeding and eternal weight. To live in those scales is to live in the kingdom’s register and to find the daily life ordered accordingly.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kābōd (weight, heaviness; the great word that becomes glory) and kābēd (to be heavy, weighty); Greek baros (weight, heaviness; 2 Cor 4:17, “eternal weight of glory”) and doxa (glory; the NT equivalent of kābōd).

expand to see more

Hebrew kābōd (H3519) — weight, heaviness, glory (the great theological substantive).

Hebrew kābēd (H3513) — to be heavy, weighty, glorious (the verb).

Greek baros (G922) — weight, heaviness (2 Cor 4:17, “eternal weight of glory”).

Greek doxa (G1391) — glory (the NT translation of kābōd); inseparable from the weight category.

Usage

"To glorify God is to give Him weight; to despise Him is to count Him light—the doxological grammar is the weight grammar."

"Our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory—the eschatological scales reverse the present sense of weight."

"Digital-age lightness dulls the soul’s capacity to feel the true weight of God, the soul, and eternity; recovery is partly negative (reduce trivializing inputs) and partly positive (sustained presence with heavy realities)."
